App Shell Architect

Act as a senior teaching assistant. Propose a minimal Next.js App Router + TypeScript + Tailwind starter for a neighborhood property platform with three feature cards: listings, neighborhood sponsors, and planned voice help. Give a file plan, terminal commands, accessibility requirements, and a verification checklist. Never invent command results or credentials. Do not include secrets or private data. Use fictional examples only.

First explain the proposed stack in plain language for a student and identify what each tool does. Then provide the minimal plan and commands, followed by accessibility and verification checks. Keep source code to short illustrative snippets rather than a giant code dump. Distinguish fresh-project creation from repairing an existing inherited repository; never overwrite existing teammate history. Note version-sensitive commands and anything that must be checked against official documentation. This is a proposed teaching plan; no command is being run by you.

App Shell Architect: Neighborhood Property Platform Teaching plan | Next.js App Router + TypeScript + Tailwind CSS 1. Understanding the proposed stack We will design a small website called NeighborNest, a fictional neighborhood property platform. The goal is to build a clean, accessible homepage with three feature cards without introducing unnecessary complexity. The starter uses three core technologies: Technology What it does Why we need it Next.js React framework for building websites and handling routes Provides the App Router, page layouts, and development server TypeScript JavaScript with type checking Helps catch mistakes before the app runs Tailwind CSS Utility-based CSS styling system Makes it easier to build responsive layouts We will also use React for reusable interface components, Node.js to run development tools, npm to manage packages, ESLint to check code quality, and Git to track changes. Think of Next.js as the building's structure, TypeScript as the blueprint checker, and Tailwind as the interior design toolkit. 2. Proposed homepage NeighborNest Home Discover your neighborhood Explore local homes, discover community sponsors, and find helpful resources. Listings Explore fictional homes. Sponsors Meet local partners. Voice Help Coming soon. Conceptual homepage preview — not a running Next.js application. The initial version will be a static frontend. No database, authentication, payment processing, live listings, or microphone access is needed. 3. Minimal file plan Next.js App Router uses folders and special files to organize pages. neighbornest/ src/ app/ layout.tsx — shared HTML shell page.tsx — homepage globals.css — global styles components/ FeatureCard.tsx — reusable card public/ — optional static assets package.json — dependencies and scripts tsconfig.json — TypeScript settings .gitignore — excluded files The project generator may also create ESLint, PostCSS, and Next.js configuration files. Keep these unless there is a documented reason to change them. Short illustrative component src/components/FeatureCard.tsx TypeScript type FeatureCardProps = { title: string; description: string; }; export function FeatureCard({ title, description, }: FeatureCardProps) { return (

{title}

{description}

); } In page.tsx, use this component three times for Listings, Neighborhood Sponsors, and Voice Help. For the voice card, display Coming soon. Do not request microphone permission or pretend voice assistance is operational. 4. Terminal commands There are two different starting situations. Students should identify which one applies before making changes. Path A — Create a fresh project Use this only when starting in a new location that does not already contain a project. Bash node --version npm --version npx create-next-app@latest neighbornest cd neighbornest npm run dev During interactive setup, choose TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, ESLint, App Router, and a src/ directory. The import alias @/* is convenient. The generator's questions and flags can change between releases. Confirm current options in the official create-next-app documentation. Check the supported Node.js version in the current Next.js installation guide before proceeding. Once the development server starts successfully, the terminal should provide a local address, typically http://localhost:3000. This is an expected address, not an observed result. Path B — Repair an inherited repository If the project already exists, do not run the project generator over it. First inspect its current state: Bash pwd git status git branch --show-current git log -5 --oneline ls -la Review package.json, the lockfile, existing routes, and any README or teammate instructions. If the repository uses npm and has a valid package-lock.json, the usual reproducible installation command is: Bash npm ci Only after reviewing the repository and preserving existing changes should you create a feature branch, when appropriate: Bash git switch -c feature/neighborhood-shell Do not delete .git, reset teammate commits, force-push, overwrite uncommitted files, or replace the lockfile merely to make setup easier. If the repository uses pnpm or Yarn, follow its existing package manager and documented workflow instead. 5. Accessibility requirements Accessibility should be part of the first implementation rather than added after the homepage is complete. Semantic HTML: Use

. Keyboard support: Every interactive link or button must work without a mouse and have a visible focus indicator. Readable contrast: Aim for WCAG AA contrast: at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Responsive layout: Stack cards on smaller screens and use three columns on larger screens without horizontal scrolling. Clear labels: Use meaningful link text, accessible names, and appropriate alternative text for informative images. Hide purely decorative icons from assistive technology. Voice feature honesty: Label it as planned. Do not create a fake working button. When implemented later, provide a text-based alternative and clear microphone permission controls. A simple responsive card container might look like: TypeScript

The exact breakpoint and styling should be tested at real viewport widths. 6. Verification checklist These checks are proposed for the student to perform. No commands have been executed, and no results are being claimed. Student verification 0 of 10 complete Project setup Node.js and package manager versions satisfy the chosen Next.js release. Development server npm run dev starts and the homepage loads locally. Feature cards All three cards appear with correct fictional content. Responsive design Cards stack on narrow screens and align correctly on desktop. Keyboard navigation All active controls are reachable and focus is visible. Accessibility Headings, landmarks, labels, and text contrast are checked. Type checking npx tsc --noEmit finishes without TypeScript errors. Linting npm run lint succeeds when that script exists. Production build npm run build completes successfully. Git safety Only intended files changed; teammate history remains intact. Reset checklist Suggested verification commands: Bash npx tsc --noEmit npm run lint npm run build git diff --check git status The lint command is version-sensitive: some generated projects may not include an npm run lint script. Inspect package.json and use the configured ESLint command rather than assuming it exists. For accessibility testing, use browser keyboard navigation, automated tools such as axe DevTools, and manual checks. Automated accessibility tests alone cannot guarantee compliance. 7. Official documentation to consult Before implementing, verify the current guidance for: Next.js App Router Next.js installation and environment requirements Tailwind CSS with Next.js TypeScript WCAG 2.2 accessibility reference 8. Definition of done The teaching exercise is complete when the student can explain the stack, identify each file's purpose, display three responsive feature cards, verify accessibility basics, and demonstrate a clean TypeScript check and production build. Recommended scope: Keep the first milestone frontend-only. Use fictional listing descriptions and sponsor names, and mark voice assistance as planned. This creates a small, understandable foundation for adding real functionality later without unnecessary dependencies or exposing private information. No commands were run, no credentials were used, and no existing repository files were modified.
